items.excerpt: 08 November 2026• Update: 08 November 2026 Here’s a rundown of all the news you need to start Sunday, including Poland's interior minister's claim that far-right ideologies may have influenced a Krakow attacker; Israeli President Isaac Herzog's appointment of Gadi Eisenkot to form the next government; and the US army's announcement of a new task force to disrupt Iran's supply routes. Initial indications suggest that the suspect who opened fire in central Krakow, Poland's second-largest city, was influenced by far-right ideologies, according to Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski. Kierwinski told a news conference that police opened fire on the suspect three minutes after receiving the first report of the attack. He confirmed that six people were killed, including one foreign national, while 16 were injured, including five foreign nationals, two police officers and the suspect. - Israel’s President Herzog says he will task Eisenkot with forming next government Israeli President Isaac Herzog announced that he will task Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming the next government, Israeli news site Ynet reported. Eisenkot has been invited to receive the mandate at a ceremony at the President’s Residence on Sunday at 5 pm local time (1500GMT), according to the report. Once he receives the mandate, Eisenkot will have 28 days to form a government. Herzog can grant an extension of up to 14 days under Israel’s Basic Law. - US army announces new task force to disrupt Iran’s supply routes The US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) announced the establishment of a new task force aimed at disrupting Iran’s use of land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials, expanding Washington’s pressure on Tehran. In a statement on US social media platform X, CENTCOM said Adm. Brad Cooper, the command’s chief, directed the formation of Task Force Iron Gate on Nov. 7. The unit, comprising approximately 20 civilian and military personnel, will be based in Tampa, Florida. The task force will work with other US government agencies to monitor and prevent the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and what Washington describes as illegal revenue streams across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea.

items.title: US inflation set to cool in October after two months of sharp increases | World News - Business Standard
items.excerpt: 8 min read Last Updated : Nov 08 2026 | 1:03 PM IST By Vince Golle and Craig Stirling Prices for US goods and services probably rose at a slower pace in October after two particularly uncomfortable months for American consumers. The consumer price index is seen rising 0.3% after a 0.6% increase that was the largest since April, based on the median projection in a Bloomberg survey of economists ahead of Tuesday’s Bureau of Labor Statistics’ release. The core measure, which excludes often-volatile energy and food components, also probably cooled. The survey median sees a 0.2% increase for October, which would be the smallest advance in three months. The agency won’t publish year-over-year figures after it skipped the October 2025 CPI release due to the federal government shutdown at the time. ## The Fed is expected to hold rates steady. Warsh will have to explain why ## Fed Chair Warsh stresses price stability, offers no signals on rate outlook The October CPI will be the last before the Federal Reserve’s meeting in December, at which investors expect policymakers to boost interest rates. Economists will also assess the finer details of the report for clues on inflation risks into early 2027. Economists at Citigroup Inc. said in a recent note that they anticipate limited pass-through of high energy costs to goods prices, as well as moderate services inflation. What Bloomberg Economics Says... > “We expect headline CPI slowed to 0.25% in October (vs. 0.65% prior). The core likely softened to 0.24% (vs. 0.33% prior), with both softer goods and services price gains driving the improvement. For goods, used cars and consumer electronics — categories that have faced pressure from the AI boom — saw slower inflation. For services, gains in owners’ equivalent rent are down a third from a September spike.” > > > > —Anna Wong, Troy Durie and Eliza Winger The latest snapshot of inflation also follows Friday’s stronger-than-expected October jobs report. Sustained employment growth has the potential of ensuring consumers keep spending, while allowing the Fed to keep its focus squarely on inflation. Another price report, due on Friday, is projected to show nagging inflationary pressures faced by companies. The producer price index is forecast to accelerate to 6.6% for the year through October, the steepest annual increase in nearly four years.

items.title: Fed policymakers consider rate hike after strong jobs report - The Korea Herald
items.excerpt: Published : Nov. 8, 2026 - 10:24:06 ... A stronger-than-expected US jobs report bolstered the case for further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes, which had lost some momentum ‌amid a post-election stock market selloff and growing fears that weaker AI-driven demand could undercut the economy. Employers added 165,000 jobs last month, more than twice what economists had expected, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said Friday, and the unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1 percent. Average hourly wages gained 3.1 percent from a year earlier, not enough to keep up with a 3.7 percent rise in consumer prices that is ‌taking a bigger chunk of the typical paycheck's purchasing power. After the US central bank left its policy rate on hold last month, Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said policymakers would be watching for "the accumulation of data" to help decide whether more monetary policy tightening would be needed. For San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, the latest monthly jobs report appeared to put a definitive tick in the "yes" column. "People are just at the point where they're — they say 'Inflation — I'm doing well ⁠in everything, except I can't keep up with inflation,' so that has to be our number one priority, and the fact that we have a solid labor market gives us the latitude, really, to just get that job done," Daly said in an interview on CNBC. "My expectation is, we're going to have to tighten policy further," said Daly, who is not a voting member of the Fed's policy committee this ⁠year but typically voices views similar to the majority view. Noting "how volatile the world seems to be in many ways," she added, "those volatilities are something that you have to take into account, collect more information, and be deliberate but more gradual in how you get there when you don't know exactly where you're going to need to head. But more is likely to be ​needed and certainly we're prepared — I'm prepared — to do that, if that's what the economy calls for." In comments at a St. Louis civic event Friday, St. ‌Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said inflation remained the top concern in his conversations with businesses in his district. "Inflation is a regressive tax, a distortionary tax," said Musalem, who has advocated for further rate ‌increases. "The best thing we can do for growth ‌and employment is bring inflation back down on a timely basis." ... The ‌release of the latest employment report, however, put a Fed rate hike back in focus. Markets were pricing about an 80 percent chance of a quarter-percentage-point policy rate increase at the Fed's December 8-9 meeting, up from about 67 percent Thursday. Traders now also see the next and final rate increase coming earlier, in April instead of June, as the central bank battles inflation that has been running above its 2 percent target for more than ​five years. "This is a very strong labor market report on the heels of solid GDP and consumer spending data last week, reinforcing the economy's positive momentum," Olu Sonola, an analyst at Fitch Ratings, wrote after the report. Recent concern over AI poses a risk to that outlook, Sonola said, "but for now the economy remains on firm footing. The labor market's resilience keeps the Fed focused on inflation and pushes the policy debate further toward a December rate hike."

items.title: US inflation, housing and jobs: 4 key economic updates to watch this week - The Times of India
items.excerpt: ## US inflation: October CPI and PPI figures in focus The first major update will come on Tuesday, when the US releases its consumer price index (CPI) data for October. Economists expect inflation to rise to 3.9%, against 3.7% in September. The CPI tracks price movements across a broad range of goods and services. Inflation has remained above 3% since March, following the start of the US war with Iran in February. The conflict led to a sharp rise in energy prices, which pushed up petrol prices and shipping costs. Businesses will also get a fresh reading of their costs on Friday, when the October producer price index (PPI) is released. Unlike the CPI, the PPI measures price changes before goods and services reach consumers. The September PPI report had recorded its biggest increase since December 2022. It also showed how higher fuel costs, particularly for diesel, were feeding into shipping and warehousing expenses. However, crude prices fell sharply over the past week after the US midterm elections. Some believe Democrats, who routed President Donald Trump's GOP, will push to end the Iran conflict, which has sent energy prices soaring.

items.title: U.S. Companies' Inflation Concerns Reach Highest Level in Over Two Years | Aju Press
items.excerpt: U.S. companies' concerns about inflation have surged to their highest level in over two years. Rising oil prices, increased raw material costs, and logistics expenses are intensifying cost pressures on businesses, drawing attention to key U.S. inflation indicators set to be released this week. In last month's series of third-quarter earnings reports, inflation was a central topic. According to Bloomberg, companies in the S&P 500 mentioned the term 'inflation' 820 times during their October earnings conference calls, marking the highest monthly count since February 2024. In the first week of November, mentions of inflation by companies have already surpassed the total for November of last year, Bloomberg reported. By sector, industrial companies, which include machinery, equipment, construction, and transportation, had the highest number of inflation mentions at 213. Basic materials companies, including steel, chemicals, and metals, followed with 135 mentions. This reflects companies' concerns about rising production and operational costs due to raw material and energy prices, as well as logistics expenses. The impact of inflation is also spreading to consumer goods companies. U.S. automaker General Motors (GM) projected that rising raw material, logistics, and memory semiconductor prices will lead to approximately $2 billion in additional costs this year. Of this, about $400 million is attributed to inflation, with most of the impact expected in the fourth quarter. As companies face increasing cost burdens, there are concerns that price pressures at the production stage will transfer to consumer prices. If inflationary trends strengthen again, it could influence the Federal Reserve's monetary policy. According to the CME FedWatch on November 6, futures markets reflect a 76.33% probability that the Fed will raise interest rates by 0.25 percentage points at its December Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting, up from 66.9% the previous day. Inflation pressures are expected to be confirmed in key U.S. inflation indicators to be released this week. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for October will be published on November 10, with expectations of a 0.3% increase from the previous month, a slowdown from September's 0.6% rise. However, due to a government shutdown in October 2025, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) was unable to collect price survey data, so year-over-year comparisons will not be available this time. On November 13, the Producer Price Index (PPI) for October will be released. Bloomberg anticipates that the October PPI will rise by 6.6% compared to the same month last year, exceeding the previous month's increase of 6.3%. If market forecasts hold true, this would represent the highest level in nearly four years. The PPI, also known as wholesale prices, reflects changes in the prices received by companies for producing and selling goods and services. Increases in production stage prices can affect companies' costs and selling prices, ultimately impacting consumer prices, making it a key indicator for gauging inflation trends.

Trump, who campaigned on the idea that a Democratic victory in the midterms would trigger a 1929-style economic depression, has maintained that the economy is booming. Since his party lost in Tuesday's voting, he has claimed he is willing to work with Democrats in the House and Senate, though that's not something he has done much of in the past.
